speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 43 I ask unanimous consent of the House to propose a motion for the purpose of discussing a specific and important matter requiring urgent consideration. This matter concerns the administrative responsibility of the government to the Indians of northern Alberta. The Indian students have been withheld from school and parents have protested the school facilities provided for their children and have requested the minister responsible to meet with them to discuss improvement of the school facilities as well as living conditions.
Yesterday 200 Indians demonstrated outside the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Resources office at St. Paul. A further meeting has been called for Sunday. Government officials and the minister have been asked to attend. These grievances cannot be permitted to escalate. Therefore I propose to move, seconded by the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Yewchuk):
That this House instruct the minister to meet with the Indians of northern Alberta and the bands affected immediately.

I have here a report of the submission made by the minister of agriculture of the government of Manitoba to the parliamentary committee which dealt with this question. He summarizes his idea of what a real income stabilization plan for prairie grain producers should be. The report reads:
1.	The plan should provide for a net income guarantee to grain producers on a basic quantity of production or on a basic acreage.
I want members opposite to listen. He is talking about a net income guarantee, not a gross income guarantee. Farmers are not responsible if the cost of gasoline goes up, for example. They are not responsible if the cost of farm implements goes up. The government is responsible. After all, a few years ago the government appointed a royal commission headed by Professor Barber of the University of Manitoba to look into the high cost of farm implements. It was a very expensive royal commission. It reported more than a year ago but none of its recommendations have been carried out. They have been completely ignored. I wonder whether government inaction in connection with this report has anything to do with the size of the contributions the implement-making companies make to the Liberal party at election time.

The minister of agriculture of Manitoba further said:
2.	The plan should not be detrimental to efficient practices or destructive of initiative.
3.	The plan must be conducive to sound land use practices by providing for crop flexibility.
4.	The plan must be such that it is in the direct financial interest of the Government of Canada to take effective measures to reduce the cost of inputs to prairie farmers.
The question is: does the legislation before us in any way meet the criteria set out by the Manitoba minister of agriculture? The minister says the basis upon which prairie grain receipts will be stabilized in the first five years of the plan will be about 65 per cent of the average of the late 'sixties; about 70 per cent of 90 per cent of total receipts in that period. I come from an industrial riding. I know what Liberal members who represent urban constituencies would say if the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) brought in an amendment to the Labour Code increasing the minimum wage for all workers under federal jurisdiction, and if he were to announce that the minimum wage would be at the rate of 90 per cent of the wage of the last five years. He would be laughed out of office. Nevertheless, the minister has enough gall to make that kind of proposal for farmers. I say the farmers of Canada are entitled to the same consideration as are urban workers. Second, the agriculture minister of Manitoba points out that the net cost to the federal treasury in the first five years of the plan proposed by the federal government will be less than $30 million. He further contends that the stabilization account could show a surplus of at least $100 million and, possibly, $225 million by 1976. That money would be in the fund, not in the pockets of the farmers as the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) so dishonestly suggested the other night on television.

Mr. Speaker, I intend to deal with two aspects of the amendments now before the House. Before Your Honour gives me the instruction that my remarks are not relevant, I should say that I think the last few moments will prove that they are. I have been prompted to make these points by questions that were asked outside this House, particularly by backbenchers from parts of the nation other than the Prairies. Members of the press gallery have also asked similar questions and members of this House have received numerous letters from people across Canada, though particularly from the Prairies, to the effect that they find this bill very confusing. Most people do not understand it. Neither do they understand the amendments now before the House at the present time. I shall have more to say about those later, but at this point may I say there is no doubt that the bill is confusing.
I am sure all members of the House, as well as everyone on the Prairies, agree that there is need for a stabilization of the economy on the Prairies and would welcome a bill with reasonable provisions that made this possible. I say that because various members of the House have put on the record DBS figures indicating that five years ago the
October 6, 1971

average income of the farmer on the western prairies was in the neighbourhood of $5,000, whereas last year it had dropped to about $1,000, quite a drastic drop in the income of farmers in that region, as hon. members have pointed out.
Many words have been uttered in this House on the unemployment situation in eastern Canada, particularly in industrial areas. I think part of the reason for this vast unemployment presently in the land is the lack of purchasing power on the part of the farmers, and this lack is felt all across Canada.
The second question that was asked by the group to which I referred related to the accusations of filibuster and obstruction which are hurled across the floor of the House from one party to another. This they do not understand and are beginning to wonder who is responsible for this obstruction and filibustering.

I hope I shall be able to reveal to the House just who is responsible for the filibustering, but to do so one must understand this question and see it in its right light. The reason so much interest is stirred in this House when farming or agricultural legislation is presented to us is that we from the western prairies have to live with a one industry economy, namely agriculture. Of necessity, every member of the House from the Prairies, regardless of party, is very interested in any topic that relates to this industry upon which we in Western Canada depend so much.
In my own area the industry is broken down into two parts. While 50 per cent of the farmers' income comes from wheat sales, in the main, the other 50 per cent comes from livestock sales. If I were permitted to do so, I should like to say something about the government's intervention in this particular field, but I do not think this would come within the scope of the amendments. I therefore notice your glance, Mr. Speaker, and heed your warning. So the reason every member of the House from the Prairies makes the subject of agriculture his prime concern is that, as I said before, we have a one industry economy on the Prairies.
Another question that is asked is: Who actually is blocking this legislation, rather than, who appears to be blocking it? I think this point was made by my colleague from across the way. Why the necessity for a long debate on each agricultural issue to come before the House? I wish to prove that it is not the members of the opposition but the Liberal government that is responsible for the obstruction and the filibustering that appears to be taking place.
To prove my point I should like to refer to a Canadian Press release which appeared in the Ottawa Journal on October 5. The hon. member for Fraser Valley East (Mr. Pringle), who is one of the Liberal backbenchers who spoke on this amendment said, as reported in that newspaper, that the bill had flaws in it. I think other members than that hon. member have made the same statement. I think the minister in charge of the Wheat Board, if he has
Prairie Grain Stabilization Act
not made that statement, has implied there are flaws in the bill. This is one of the causes of the filibustering.
Members in this House, and certainly the people of this country, wonder why the government does not bring in amendments to correct these admitted flaws in the bill. Common sense dictates that if such action were taken much of the debate in this House of Commons would be eliminated, because we would not have to point out time and time again that these flaws are there and should be changed before the bill becomes an act. The minister, as almost everyone in this House knows, is so adamant and arrogant in his position that he will not acknowledge the weak points outlined by members even of his own party. I see the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Richardson) in the House. He spoke on this bill yesterday and I should like to make a few references to what he said. He said that the bill lacked many necessary and beneficial features desired by farmers. After saying that, he shrugged it off by saying the government would look after these omissions at a later date.

Mr. Speaker, if I had the wrong impression of what the minister said I apologize. I sat here and listened to what he said, and I was under the impression he admitted there was something lacking in the stabilization bill. In addition, he was asking the opposition to bear with the government and it would bring in these other policies later on. During previous Parliaments, the opposition has accepted similar statements made by ministers of the cabinet, but attached little significance to commitments made by backbenchers. Prior to this government taking office such a statement by a minister was accepted as government policy. That is not the case at the present time. The just society boys destroyed that king of co-operation by bringing in what is now called the "supergroup". The cabinet ministers appear to us on this side of the House to be only figureheads who take their instructions from that supergroup in the Prime Minister's office. The word of a cabinet minister is not held in such high regard today as it was in the days of previous governments.
The western members and the farmers they represent no longer trust this government, and certainly have no faith in the promises it makes. This distrust is founded on past experience of broken promises by members of this cabinet. I could list many of them. Just a few minutes ago reference was made to a broken agreement between the three prairie agriculture ministers and the federal government. There has been some explanation by the minister in charge of the Wheat Board to the effect that he did not make any agreement with the three prairie ministers, but there was an apparent misunderstanding on the part of all who took part in those discussions. We heard a moment

October 6, 1971
Prairie Grain Stabilization Act
ago from a representative of the NDP from Manitoba that his interpretation of the agreement was there would be a cease-fire for a week. Certainly, that has not been the case. I do not think any explanation by the government could convince the farmers that an agreement was not broken. This is something that has happened on past occasions, but not nearly as often. It is quite common for this government not to keep promises.
Not very long ago the minister who represents the livestock sector of the agricultural economy of western Canada broke a promise to the producers. It is for this reason I suggest the ministers of this cabinet have no power whatsoever. All the power is focused in the Prime Minister's office with that supergroup. The ministers take their instructions from that group which is telling them how to run the country. That supergroup is not even an elective group.

speechtext: It is shameful the way they forget about western Canada.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENTS TO WESTERN CANADA PRODUCERS IN YEARS WHEN RECEIPTS BELOW FIVE-YEAR AVERAGE
speechtext:
I doubt if they could get elected. Perhaps a worse feature than this broken promise is the breaking of the law in respect of payments owing to grain producers under the Temporary Wheat Reserves Act. I will not say more about that, but let me point out that in recent weeks I have stated on three different occasions that this government, as a result of a decision by the supergroup, cabinet ministers or the government as a whole, has broken faith with the country. No wonder there are accusations of filibustering and obstruction.
Many uninformed members of this House and members of the Press Gallery do not understand what we are talking about because this bill is very confusing to many, including myself. We do not know its implications, but we are afraid of certain of its features. The farmers I represent had an annual income of about $5,000 some five years ago. That annual income has now dropped to about $1,000. This government wishes to stabilize this income at $1,000 a year. That is how I read this bill. There is little need to point out that this type of action on the part of the government invites obstruction. We all know such action delays the passage of any legislation, beneficial or otherwise.
Before this government came into power, governments of the day, regardless of which party was involved, would accept suggestions by opposition members and others which would improve legislation. Other governments accepted amendments to improve bills. That type of cooperation eliminated much of the type of debate that has taken place in this House during the last three years.
This dictatorial administration demands that we pass legislation as it is presented by the government or it will withdraw the legislation. This government is not going to threaten most members on this side, regardless of party affiliation. It is no wonder people in Canada are asking what is happening to the Parliament of Canada. Even we who sit here are wondering what is happening.
In yesterday's Ottawa Journal the minister in charge of the Wheat Board is reported as having said that he would withdraw the bill. The report reads:

Mr. Lang said last week he would withdraw the bill if the opposition continued a series of procedural attacks stalling its passage.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I have news for the minister. He had better withdraw the bill forthwith and scrap it at least until such time as he comes to his senses, gets down from his high and mighty pedestal, listens to reason and accepts some of the suggestions of the farmers. I suggest to the Prime Minister that there should be a change in the cabinet, particularly in respect of the portfolio relating to the Wheat Board, because if the minister's attitude does not change and if his rigid and inflexible position continues, I believe that he must acknowledge what everyone else in this country knows, namely, that he is not capable of piloting this bill through the House of Commons. If there is no flexibility in the minister's present position, I forewarn that there are some members in this House who are determined to stall the bill in its present form.
If the minister has decided that the bill is to remain as presented, then any debate from now on is useless in the face of that adamant stand. He would perhaps be doing the Parliament of Canada a service by immediately taking the action he has threatened to implement as reported in the newspaper article because we have now reached a deadlock. Members on this side are determined to stall this legislation until the minister accepts some amendments. By his actions and by his words, he indicates that he does not intend to accept any amendments. The members to whom I referred a moment ago intend to use, regardless of what the minister says, every legal means available to them, be it procedural or otherwise to prevent the income of their constituents being stabilized, as I said before, at a poverty level. In this same press release in the Ottawa Journal, the minister is also reported as saying that the amendment is unworkable and so on. I recall a former minister of a Liberal government making a similar statement in respect of cash advances for farm stored grain. He said it was unworkable and could not be made to work. The people of Canada thought otherwise. They changed the government and proved it could be done.
Cash advances on farm stored grain became a very important piece of legislation. So, do not let the minister try to fool us that this is not workable. We would be quite satisfied if the income level were up where it should be. Stabilization should not be at a poverty level. Perhaps there are some people on the back benches and in the press gallery who believe the government has all the answers, and that nobody should listen to the opposition members. I know there are some who believe this. Those of us who do not agree with such a conclusion have a suggestion to make. Let the government listen to the Canadian citizens who will be directly affected by these amendments, as well as by the bill itself. Let us imagine for a moment a situation which, if it took place, would result in the elimination of all opposition members in this House. Who would or should the government consult? As I have said before, they should consult those people who would be affected by the legislation.
I have in my hand a telegram from the delegates of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool, District Four which is in my area. I should like to put this on the record.

This is quite reasonable. We can accept this.
2.	An adequate two price system for wheat.
This has been talked about time and time again. The people of western Canada for years and years have believed there is a double standard in Canada. There was a bill which passed through this House very quickly during this session of Parliament. I refer to the bill granting $80 million to industries in the event that some employees of certain industries were laid off. The farmers have no objection to this type of action. They say, however, that no jobs have been lost yet and the government has voted $80 million to help people who may be laid off. In God's name why can they not give us the money that is owing to us?
I could go on and mention the price of bread and so on. We have heard time and time again that an increase of 60 cents in the price of wheat would represent an increase of only one cent on a loaf of bread. We have heard some opinions expressed that labour people would not stand for this. I am not sure what the price of bread is today. It has increased by one cent, by one cent and by one cent. We have heard no complaints about this except from individual housewives. We have heard no organized complaint about this. It has been said that perhaps labour is entitled to this amount of money because of inflation and so on. Why cannot similar consideration be given to the people who produce the wheat? We have no hesitation in adopting item No. 2.
The next proposal reads as follows:
3.	Recognition of a storage policy for each kind of grain paid for jointly by government and producers.
It I had more time I should like to inform the House about the storage policy in the United States. The farmers there have no difficulty disposing of their grain whenever they want to do so. The government stores it. The system works wonderfully. I have records to show that the United
Prairie Grain Stabilization Act
States has sold proportionately almost twice as much grain as we have in the past 20 years. Australia has beaten our efforts. Why? Because our system must be antiquated and should be altered. Why should we not follow the system adopted by one of these successful countries. I have no hesitation in accepting the third proposal.
Then, we have their next proposal, which reads:
4.	An annual separate pool for each kind of grain guaranteed.
We can accept all these recommendations. This is why I say I have no hesitation in adopting the resolution passed by the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool, District Four. Much has been said about who in the Prairies supports the government view. I think the same newspaper was referred to time and time again. It lists three organizations dealing with grains that do support the minister's story, and the president of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool is one of the three but there are doubts about the first one. However, this advertisement is erroneous because the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix dated October 4 contains an article in which the president of this organization refutes the contention of the one Liberal in the city of Regina who says that the president of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool endorses the stabilization bill C-244 which the minister has presented to the House. In the president's own press release he says:
We have not endorsed, and will not endorse the proposed income stabilization plan because in our view it is inadequate. We think the stabilization of income from grains is a good idea. However, endorsation of the principle of the stabilizing of income does not mean support of the existing plan.
He also said:
.. . there is no justification for holding up money promised to farmers.
In addition, he said:
We do not support the stabilization plan as it is, nor do we want to retain the TWRA as it is.
He said nothing more than the members of the opposition have said. We want a stabilization plan. Possibly we will vote for the minister's plan if, as I said before, he will come to his senses, listen to reason, and accept some of the amendments, not amendments that we want but those that farmers themselves want. Is that asking too much?

I have a few comments to make and also a suggestion. First, I want to say that I support the motion as clarified and improved by the amendment. However, we cannot look at the amendment without putting it in context with the general situation because this amendment, like some of the others, goes to the heart of the issue. I, like other hon. members, have been west. I have looked upon the face of western agriculture in the last few months and I have found it a sad and disheartening experience in view of what used to be the situation. There is no doubt that the people who have brought this about are the people who sit opposite, and they are unfit to govern this country because of what has happened. There

October 6, 1971
Prairie Grain Stabilization Act
will be another time and another opportunity to enlarge on that aspect.
It has been suggested by the minister in charge of the Wheat Board and by others that there are stalling tactics, there is delay and there is fillibustering. These dainty dilettantes in democracy do not understand the purpose of the democratic structure in this House. It is based upon the adversary system. When an issue is thrown on the floor of the House to be contested-it is an issue in this case moved by the government- the only way in which it can be examined effectively and dealt with is through the adversary system. Therefore, we on this side of the House, and hopefully some day members on the other side when they find the intestinal fortitude to stand up for the things they believe in, will contest the validity of the proposals brought forward by the government, just as hon. members to my left are doing with this amendment and just as we are doing with many other useful-I could almost say more useful-amendments that we are offering. It is in that sense that this debate has been conducted.
I am shocked and amazed to hear it suggested that the form which this debate has taken constitutes a delay of the proceedings in this House. My hon. friends opposite are guilty of deception I think when they say "let the bill come to a vote". Unless there has been some change, we know what that means, that the obedient group on the other side will vote as they are told. I think we should bear in mind that they do not represent the majority of the voters in the 1968 election, and I think that is something which should be considered.
However, be that as it may, in pursuit of our democratic duty we have, through the means of this amendment which has been supported by members in our party, indicated the grievous faults in the case made by the government. It would be one thing if it was the government against the opposition on the basis of the adversary system of which I speak. But on the scales of truth and justice upon which we and the people of this country must balance which side is the right side there has been placed against the government the statements and the evidence of impartial and objective people who are not involved in the day to day arguments in the House of Commons.
My good friend, the hon, member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. McIntosh) gave witness to that a short time ago when he read the resolution which had come to him from his province. But over and above that, what do we find? I discount the statement of the minister in charge of the Wheat Board. I also received letters from Saskatchewan, mainly from Saskatoon, which promoted the rapid passage of this bill. Upon examining the envelope in which these letters came I find they are mainly from the city of Saskatoon, from urban farmers in that city who have been cultivating the 40 feet in their back lane.

I do not know about the minister's staff, but I certainly know that I examined those that came to me. There were so few that I had a chance to examine them carefully and in detail. Anybody who is motivated by correspondence of this kind does not deserve to sit in the House of Commons. In addition to the farmers, there are the farm organizations. All the responsible and major

farm organizations have said that they support, amongst others, an amendment of this kind; that they are not in favour of the bill in its present form and that there should be major changes before the stabilization program is made effective. These are farm organizations and the pools. In addition to that, there are the provincial ministers of agriculture, two of them comparatively new in their jobs; men who have just been through the rigours of a campaign. I was involved on the fringes of the campaign in Alberta, and let us not suggest that to some extent federal issues were extraneous to those campaigns. I do not know about Saskatchewan, but certainly in Alberta some of the federal legislation was very germane to some of the campaign fights in rural constituencies. I heard mentioned on many occasions Bill C-176 and Bill C-244, and the sad and pitiful showing of the Liberal party at that time. The success of our party indicates beyond any doubt that the farm organizations, the farmers, the prairie premiers and the prairie ministers of agriculture are opposed to this bill in its present form.
Under those conditions, it would be manifestly absurd for the government to suggest that we should not make it quite plain that we propose to support the amendment put forward for the purpose of improving the legislation. The facts are simple, Mr. Speaker. The bill is not adequate and must be changed. But the government, like most governments, is unwilling to make changes because the changes are proposed from this side of the House. Probably the minister would like a long delay with the opportunity to propose changes himself. But we cannot trust the government. We cannot trust these ministers. We have seen what happened with respect to a simple understanding that consideration of the bill would be postponed under certain conditions. Those conditions were not met.
Be that as it may, and in the belief that what the government is seeking is a face-saving device, I wish to make a suggestion before the vote is called. I make it on my own behalf. I am not authorized to make it on behalf of my party, but I think it has merit. If the government is really interested in providing a stabilization measure which will be effective and useful to the people of western Canada, then in the first instance I suggest it should immediately pay the money it owes under Chapter 2 of the 1956 statutes, the Temporary Wheat Reserves Act, and the Canadian Wheat Board should then pay to the farmers the amount which it owes them, on the normal basis. There can be no alternative to this. The government has been in default. It has broken the law. This situation has gone on for 14 or 15 months. There is no other way in which the government can purge its contempt and make itself respectable again.
My second suggestion is made on the assumption that the bill will pass. The government has the troops, the bodies-I was almost going to say the willing, dumb bodies, but I will just say the willing bodies-to compel passage of the bill. I imagine that having secured consent from his colleagues the minister intends to persist with the bill until it is passed. I also assume that the government is going to reject all of the useful and valid amendments that have been proposed. This being the case, I suggest that the minister make use of the amendment
October 6, 1971

which he has placed on the order paper. I suggest that when the bill does pass clause 32 should be immediately proclaimed. This is the clause which provides for the payment of $100 million. I suggest that then the balance of the clauses of the bill should not be implemented.
I suggest that the implementation of the balance of the clauses should be delayed for some considerable time. In fact, I assume that the minister has no intention of operating the new provisions at least until the new crop year arrives. I suggest that the order in council containing the proclamation bringing the rest of the clauses of the bill into effect should be delayed until there has been an honest, valid and meaningful attempt by the government to secure, in co-operation with the farm organizations, farmers, provincial governments and the opposition parties, a form of stabilization bill that will work, that is acceptable, and does not contain the repugnant provisions of the present bill.
How in the name of heaven can the government be satisfied that this bill will meet the real requirements of the farm population of western Canada? In the light of what has been said by the farm organizations, by members of the New Democratic Party, by members of this party, and by the prairie ministers of agriculture, which I assume the minister must have taken to heart, how can the government be honestly and truthfully satisfied that this bill meets the needs of the prairie farmers? If the government genuinely desires such a result, and I have not completely ruled out that possibility at this stage, then what I suggest could very easily be brought about as the means to secure it. But because I do not trust the government any more, I would insist that any order in council implementing the remaining provisions of the bill should not come into effect until an affirmative resolution was introduced in this House, and debated without time limitation.
These proposals are simple. As I say, I make them on my own behalf, as some indication of what might be worked out if there is any real, honest, genuine intent on the part of the government to try to do something for the people of western Canada. speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I believe I was pointing out that the main principle of this bill is the provision of stabilization payments to farmers under certain conditions, conditions that we regard as too severe. In order for farmers who are growing any of the six grains covered by this bill to receive payments, a year must be so bad that the total income in the area covered by the bill is less than 90 per cent of the average total income of the preceding five years.
When one realizes that, among other factors, there is the fact that the cost of production has gone up, it can readily be seen that, if in any such difficult year the farmers do not get paid unless their gross income falls below the five year, this will have the effect of precluding the making of payments under the stabilization fund for many years. Gross income could be a very large figure whereas the actual net income of the farmer, because of increased costs of production, could be below the average income of the previous five years, and yet no payments would be made to the farmers. That is why we feel very strongly about this bill and that is why these amendments are still before the House. We feel the bill should be amended to right this provision, namely that stabilization payments out of the fund to the farmers will come into effect in any year when the net income of the farmer falls below the average of the preceding five years.
We would also like to change the 90 per cent figure and other things, but we do feel that this principle of distinguishing between the gross income and the net income is one that is extremely important to the successful operation of this bill. Again, I remind the minister that the organizations representing the farmers of western Canada are putting this point as number one in the pleas they are now making to the government. I suggest it is just possible that the farm organizations might understand the situation and might know what is best for the farmer, and I think the minister ought to pay attention to their pleas.
I know, this House being constituted as it is, and in view of the vote we have just had, that if this amendment comes to a vote and the government says it has to be turned down it will be turned down. If we simply go on and put the bill on the statute books, the effect will be to
Prairie Grain Stabilization Act
provide a bill that will not do what its sponsors say it is supposed to do. It will not be a piece of legislation that will stabilize farm income in western Canada. It will not be a bill to even out the humps and hollows, it will be merely a bill which will result in the farmers putting millions of dollars into a fund for one purpose, namely that in a catastrophic year payments will come out of the fund for the farmer. That will not be satisfactory, and I urge that consideration be given to this amendment.
Like the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), who spoke a while ago when we were on the previous amendment, I should like to make some suggestions to the minister and to the government. As I have already said, if this comes to a vote and the government says it must be turned down that will be the end of the amendment. As the minister knows, representations are still being made to him and to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) for further consultation about this bill. The minister and the Prime Minister have been invited to go out west to meet officers of the National Farmers Union and the wheat pools and, despite some difficulty there was today as to whether Thanksgiving weekend is the time to do this, I hope these meetings will be held.
If the meetings are going to be held, surely the thing to do now is to desist from further debate on this bill in the House of Commons. We are not asking the government to withdraw the bill in the sense that it be removed from the order paper, but we are asking the government to let the bill stand. The government has other things it wants to proceed with, including the tax bill and a few other items, and this is the purpose of our continuing the debate at this time, to plead with the government to let this bill stand in order that consideration can be given to ways in which the bill can be improved.
Although there have been difficulties in the past day or two, so far as the Chair is concerned, about hon. members staying in order when speaking on the amendment, I submit there should be no difficulty about staying in order on the part of those who speak in respect of this amendment because it touches the very heart of this bill; is it to be confined by this reference to gross income so its benefits will never flow to the farmer, or is it to be a measure based on net income that will help get the benefits to the farmer in a way that will even out the humps and hollows?
It has been said in the course of this debate that the principle of stabilization legislation is good. We confirm that, for we believe there should be legislation to stabilize farm income in western Canada. We think it should be on a rational basis which holds out the prospect of raising the level of living in western Canada, not just stabilizing it at the poverty level, or perhaps a level that is declining. We think a rational stabilization plan should be worked out. We do not think this bill does that. It is tied to this $100 million carrot, as it were, and it is mixed up with this whole question of whether the Temporary Wheat Reserves Act money should be paid out.
We suggest that the whole thing has got into a mess which should not be continued any longer. Let me say that we agree with the contention from the other side, indeed from both sides of the House, that there should be stabilization legislation, but despite its title we think this legislation is not that kind of legislation. We also agree with the

October 6, 1971
Prairie Grain Stabilization Act
other side that the whole question of how we provide for storage of surplus grain in western Canada, not just wheat but all six of the major grains, is one that is not adequately covered by the Temporary Wheat Reserves Act. We do not think that is a piece of perfect legislation which must stay for all time. We think there must be a new policy in regard to the way in which we provide for the cost of storing surplus grain.
By the way, that is another of the main points of the representations farm organizations are making to the government at this time. They not only want net income as the base rather than gross income, a two-price system and a few other things, they want the whole policy regarding storage costs to be put on a rational basis. To narrow all this to two things, what is before us in this bill is a proposal for stabilization, which is not satisfactory and will not work, and a proposal in respect of storage which simply repeals the Temporary Wheat Reserves Act without putting anything in its place.
What the farmers of western Canada, through their farm organizations, have said they want is for the government to sit down with them and work out a rational solution to these two problems. I will go as far as giving the minister credit for being aware of the fact that these two problems exist. It is clear, I admit, that purpose of this bill is to cope with those two problems. He is attempting to get something better than the Temporary Wheat Reserves Act and something in the way of stabilization, but with great respect I say he has not solved either of these problems.
In the meantime we have become lost in the battle over the payments which have not been made under the Temporary Wheat Reserves Act for 15 months. We have become lost in respect of figures and the arguments about which piece of legislation would be best and which would pay the farmers the most in the next three years. We have heard arguments about $170 million as compared to $113 million, and we have heard different figures from both sides. I think that all this proves this bill is not a satisfactory solution to these two main problems; the problem of providing for stabilization on a rational basis and the problem of providing a rational program for the payment of the cost of storing surplus grain in western Canada.
In light of all that I believe the farm organizations are being reasonable, logical and responsible in asking the government to give this matter further consideration. A Liberal member, whom I need not name, asked me earlier today if I realized that by our continuing to debate this bill we were challenging or tempting the government to withdraw it or cease to proceed with it so that it would not pass and did I not feel badly about that and realize the disastrous consequences that would flow from that. I said to him, "Do you think we are fooling around; that is precisely what we want". We want the government not to proceed with Bill C-244 in its present form, to let it lie on the order paper and to meet with the farmers of western Canada to discuss a rational and sensible solution to these problems, with a view to obtaining an adequate stabilization program that, would even out the bumps and hollows and not just take care of a serious hollow which occurs once in every 20 years. It should be evened out to provide

a decent level of income for the farmers of Western Canada.
The other problem is to do something better than the Temporary Wheat Reserves Act does in respect of the problem of grain stored in western Canada. As I say, this is a place where we can debate and have votes. I know as well as I am standing here today that if there is a vote on the amendment of the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar it will be defeated, and we will go on to debate the other 14 amendments on the order paper at the report stage. I know those amendments will be defeated and that the bill will go through in its present form. We also know around here that when legislation gets on the statute books it takes a long time to get it changed. The whole idea of improving the Temporary Wheat Reserves Act is a good one. The whole idea of a plan to stabilize farm income in western Canada is good, but if we are to cope with these two problems let us do so sensibly.

the people who are affected should be heard, and in this case that means the farmers.

Prairie Grain Stabilization Act

In support of what I have just said, one needs only refer to the explanation given yesterday, October 5, 1917 by the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Lang) in reply to a question put by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) as to whether the hon. minister knew exactly what the farmers would get under the new prairie grain stabilisation legislation, recorded on page 8446 of Hansard, from which I quote:
If we have the Temporary Wheat Reserves Act route followed, without therefore passing Bill C-244, of the $62.1 million which would be paid we know that $38.6 million would reach the farmers because that is in connection with a crop year for which the transactions are concluded. Had that amount been paid it would ordinarily have been paid on June 17 as we made quite clear at all times.
I have received perhaps 600 or 700 letters from western producers first telling me to ask the government to make the payments according to the former legislation, and afterwards, they agreed with the new legislation. Yesterday, the hon. minister said, and I quote:
The $38.6 million would therefore have reached the farmers. The balance would apply to future operations of the wheat pool as would the $30.8 million and the $20 million estimated for the subsequent years. These would apply to future wheat pools. The point I made to the hon. member who just spoke was that should any of these pools turn out to be in a deficit position, not one penny of it flows through to the farmer. So, there is no certainty possible at this time whether those amounts of money will get to the farmer. All that would happen would be that the payment by the treasury would, to that extent, reduce the treasury obligation on another account. It would not get to the farmer if the pools were in a deficit position, as it was a year ago when the Temporary Wheat Reserves Act payments did not get through to the farmers.
Mr. Speaker, such statements by the minister explain very well why western farmers are so worried about Bill C-244. In fact, they know very well that, if the June 1971 payments had been made, the situation would have been less confusing. Farmers think that this legislation is to put an end to the $38.6 million owed to them by the government under the former act.
I received today from Bonnyville, Alberta, the following letter:

As a half section of land farmer, I ask you to vote for the Prairie Grains Stabilization Act. The transitional payment I would receive would amount to $511.85. I would get much less under the Temporary Wheat Reserves Act.
Yours truly,
Denis A. Rondeau Bonnyville, Alberta.

That is as far from the truth as it is possible to get. I reject it entirely. I repeat what I said on Monday morning when this question first came up and I raised the question of privilege. At that time I said, because the government had indicated through its spokesman that a moratorium was contingent upon there being some consideration of amendments and changes to Bill C-244, this would be satisfactory. When I was told categorically that prospects for any changes were very, very remote, I made it quite plain that as far as this party was concerned, there was no objection to there being any moratorium.
Those are the facts, Mr. Speaker. I can only say that those whom the gods would destroy they first make mad.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. As was indicated when discussing this matter earlier, particularly at the time the leader of the New Democratic Party was speaking, if there had persisted to the beginning of the House sittings on Monday an agreement simply to have a moratorium on the debate and any discussion of legalities without any preconditions about what was involved or what would be assumed as a result of that moratorium, we would likely have had one.
The House leader for the official opposition has today confirmed what I suggested at that time, that the failure to obtain a moratorium was due to their insistence that their agreement depended upon our committing ourselves in advance of any discussions or conversation about the likelihood of changes being made in the bill at this time. We had to make very clear to them that it was not a likelihood at this stage. We made that clear to them. At that point they refused the moratorium on that understanding.

speechtext: I have the honour to inform the House that a message has been received from the Senate informing this House that the Senate have passed the following bill with amendments: Bill C-262, An Act to support employment in Canada by mitigating the disruptive effect on Canadian industry of the imposition of foreign import surtaxes or other actions of a like effect, to which the concurrence of this House is desired.

A message was delivered by the Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod as follows:
Mr. Speaker, the honourable the Deputy Governor General desires the immediate attendance of this honourable House in the Chamber of the honourable the Senate.
Accordingly, Mr. Speaker with the House went up to the Senate Chamber.
And being returned:
Mr. Speaker informed the House that the Deputy Governor General had been pleased to give, in Her Majesty's name, the royal assent to the following bill:
An Act to amend the Judges Act and the Financial Administration Act.
At six o'clock the House adjourned, without question put, pursuant to Standing Order.
